summary: Describes CAST-256, an existing block cipher, covering its structure, key scheduling, s-boxes and test vectors. It is informational and does not make CAST-256 a standard.

eli5.summary: It is a recipe for a secret code machine that scrambles messages in a fixed way. The document includes sample inputs and outputs to check you built it correctly.

questions: cast-256 block size and key sizes
subtitle: A 128-bit block cipher with variable key sizes from 128 to 256 bits.

tldr.problem: Internet applications need unencumbered encryption algorithms that are cryptographically strong and freely available, with support for a range of key sizes.
tldr.mechanism: CAST-256 is a block cipher using a Substitution-Permutation Network (SPN) structure built on CAST-128, with a 128-bit block size and key sizes of 128, 160, 192, 224, or 256 bits. It uses a complex key schedule and multiple rounds of keyed transformations.
tldr.outcome: CAST-256 provides a freely-available encryption algorithm with good resistance to cryptanalysis and desirable properties like avalanche effect and absence of weak keys, suitable for general-purpose Internet use.

today: RFC 2612 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. CAST-256 remains an unencumbered encryption algorithm available for use, though it is not a standard of any Internet protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
CAST-256 is a Substitution-Permutation Network (SPN) cipher built as an evolution of the CAST-128 algorithm. It operates on 128-bit blocks of data and supports variable key sizes of 128, 160, 192, 224, or 256 bits, making it flexible for different security requirements.

The cipher exhibits strong cryptographic properties including resistance to differential and linear cryptanalysis, good avalanche properties (where small input changes produce large output changes), and the Strict Avalanche Criterion. It has no complementation property and contains no weak or semi-weak keys, making it a reliable choice for general-purpose encryption throughout the Internet community.
sections.eli5: CAST-256 is a formula for scrambling 128 bits (16 characters) at a time using a secret key. It mixes the data many times in ways that depend on your secret number, following mathematical rules that make it very hard to reverse without the key.

sections.title: Algorithm Structure and Notation
sections.content:
CAST-256 operates on a 128-bit block called BETA, divided into four 32-bit quantities (A, B, C, D). The encryption process applies two phases: six forward quad-rounds (each making four keyed transformations) followed by six reverse quad-rounds that undo the structure. Decryption reverses the key order and uses the same operations in reverse.

The cipher reuses three round function types from CAST-128 (Type 1, 2, and 3), each combining a keyed mixing operation with s-box (substitution table) lookups and arithmetic operations. The key schedule expands the user key into round keys through a process using a 256-bit working block, transforming it through octave operations (eight-step transformations) to derive the rotation and masking keys needed for each round.
sections.eli5: The algorithm takes 128 bits and passes them through 12 rounds of mixing. Each round uses lookup tables and math operations to shuffle the data based on parts of your secret key. The secret key itself is processed to create different parts for each round.

sections.title: Key Schedule and Round Keys
sections.content:
The key scheduling process initializes constant values based on mathematical constants (square roots of 2 and 3), then iteratively generates rotation and masking keys. The algorithm processes the user-supplied key (padded with zeros for shorter keys) through 24 pairs of octave transformations, extracting rotation keys from the five least significant bits of specific 32-bit values and masking keys from full 32-bit values.

Rotation keys control how much data is shifted circularly in each round, while masking keys combine data through addition or XOR operations. This separation of concerns and the large number of transformation steps ensure that small differences in the key produce widely different round keys, which is essential for security.
sections.eli5: Your secret key is mixed through many steps using special numbers, creating different small pieces of the key for each round. These pieces tell the cipher how to shuffle data differently in each step.

sections.title: Round Functions and S-Boxes
sections.content:
CAST-256 uses four substitution boxes (S1, S2, S3, S4), each containing 256 entries that map byte values to 32-bit outputs. These s-boxes are pre-computed and represent the non-linear core of the algorithm. Each round function type (f1, f2, f3) uses these s-boxes differently: combining their outputs through addition, subtraction, and XOR operations in patterns specifically designed to achieve good diffusion and confusion of the input data.

The s-boxes were designed to avoid patterns that could enable cryptanalysis, ensuring that the algorithm provides good avalanche properties and resistance to both differential and linear attacks. The use of four different s-boxes in each round, combined with key-dependent operations, provides multiple layers of obfuscation.
sections.eli5: The algorithm uses four lookup tables with numbers that scramble your data in non-obvious ways. Each round picks bytes from these tables and combines them using addition and bit flipping, making the transformation different for each round.

sections.title: Cryptographic Properties and Implementation
sections.content:
CAST-256 demonstrates several important security properties. The Strict Avalanche Criterion (SAC) ensures that changing a single input bit affects approximately half of the output bits. The Bit Independence Criterion (BIC) ensures that bits affected by a single input bit are independent of each other. The absence of complementation property means that complementing the key does not simply complement the ciphertext, preventing a class of attacks.

The algorithm is available worldwide on a royalty-free and license-free basis for both commercial and non-commercial use. Appendix A of the RFC provides test vectors for validation—known answers for encryption of all-zero plaintexts with various key sizes, allowing implementers to verify their implementation against reference outputs at each round.
sections.eli5: CAST-256 has mathematical properties that make it very hard to break. It is free for anyone to use anywhere. The RFC includes test numbers that show what the right answer should be, so you can check that your copy of the algorithm works correctly.

references.text: Adams, C., "The CAST-128 Encryption Algorithm", RFC 2144, May 1997.
